extracted.intended_audience: researchers, science-communication scholars, press officers and journalists interested in health-related science press releases and their effect on news
extracted.subtask_description: Assess press releases about biomedical and health-related research for levels of advice, strength of causal claims, human inference from non-human studies, presence of caveats and justifications, and their association with news uptake and news phrasing. The rubric is applied by coding press releases, the associated peer-reviewed articles, and resulting news stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice level coding (4 categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each source (journal article, press release, news) is coded for maximum level of advice out of four categories: no advice; implicit advice (e.g. 'for adults with a BMI greater than 35 kg/m2…permanent calorie reductions…'); explicit advice but not to the reader/general public (e.g. 'clinicians must exercise caution…'); explicit advice to the reader/general public (e.g. 'patients who are at increased risk…should consider starting statin treatment').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include sets in the advice analysis only if at least one source contains implicit or explicit advice. Examples provided. Caveats and justifications for advice are coded only where explicit advice appears. Use highest level present in the source as that source's advice score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal-claim strength coding (7 levels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Main statements of findings are coded according to seven ordered levels: no statement; statement of no relationship; correlational; ambiguous; conditional causal; can cause; causal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code the title and first two sentences of press releases and news (and abstract and discussion in journal articles) because these present the main claims. Analysis focuses on correlational cross-sectional and longitudinal designs; exclude qualitative, intervention, or simulation designs. Use the first two sentences as the main-claim window since they likely have largest influence on readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human inference from non-human research
rubrics_metrics.description: For journal articles based on non-human samples (animals, cells, simulations), code the associated press release and news as: explicitly non-human, implicitly human, or explicitly human.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This coding assesses whether conclusions are presented as applicable to humans when the underlying study is non-human. Because such cases were rare, some analyses may be infeasible; report raw results when N is low.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: Binary coding of whether a press release (or news) contains a caveat qualifying a causal/correlational statement or explicit advice (e.g. 'We still need more research to clarify whether vitamin D directly prevents bowel cancer...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveats for causal statements are coded for every relevant press release; caveats for explicit advice are coded only where explicit advice appears. Combine datasets if caveats are rare to allow analysis. Analyze whether caveats affect news uptake and whether caveats in press releases predict caveats in news (odds ratios provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of justifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Binary coding of whether a press release (or news) contains justifications for causal statements or advice (e.g. explanations of why a conclusion is warranted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justifications for causal statements are coded if the PR contains any explicit statement of relationship; justifications for advice are coded only for PRs containing explicit advice. Examine associations with news uptake and whether justifications in PR predict justifications in news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration (operational definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggeration is defined as claims or advice in press releases or news that are coded at a level above any of the associated statements in the peer-reviewed journal article (the journal article serves as the baseline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This captures 'message creep' beyond the journal article text rather than absolute scientific accuracy. Do not attempt to judge whether the journal article itself is exaggerated. Use the ordered coding schemes (advice levels, causal strength, human inference) to determine whether a PR/news item is higher than the journal baseline. Report exaggeration rates and use odds ratios to assess association between PR exaggeration and news exaggeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: News uptake and reach metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure whether a press release generated any news coverage (binary news uptake) and the number of news stories resulting from each press release (count).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare proportions of PRs with and without associated news (bootstrapped 95% CIs and standard inferential tests). When multiple news stories per PR exist, adjust analyses for clustering (see analysis methods). Use these metrics to test whether exaggeration, caveats, or justifications affect news uptake or number of stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main-statement selection rule
rubrics_metrics.description: When coding, use the title and first two sentences of press releases and news stories as the location for the main statement; for journal articles use abstract and discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule is justified because main claims are typically stated first and have the greatest influence on readers. The focus is on main statements, not supporting text later in the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion/exclusion criteria for analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases were included if based on research relevant to human health, psychology or neuroscience from target journals (Lancet, BMJ, Science, Nature family journals) for 2011. Causal-claim analyses restricted to correlational cross-sectional and longitudinal designs; qualitative, intervention, and simulation designs excluded from those analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sample sizes are small for a subcategory (e.g., non-human inference), report partial or raw results and note limitations. Document source repositories (journal web pages, EurekAlert) and search strategy for associated news (Nexis, BBC, Reuters, Google).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding instrument and reliability standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a structured coding sheet with comprehensive questions (the study used 191 questions) and train coders; double-code a random subset to assess inter-coder reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record time per set (3–4 hours per set in this study). Double-coding a substantial random sample (e.g., ~25–30%) allows estimation of concordance; the study reports 98.3% concordance (κ = 0.97). Where resources are limited, prioritize increasing sample size over excessive double-coding, assuming good reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical analysis approach for clustered media data
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust statistical analyses for clustering of multiple news articles per press release and use appropriate methods to estimate associations and confidence intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study used generalized estimating equations to produce percentages and 95% CIs while adjusting for clustering (exchangeable working correlation) and to estimate odds ratios for associations (e.g., between PR exaggeration and news exaggeration). Use bootstrapped 95% CIs and standard inferential tests for analyses without clustering (e.g., news uptake binary comparisons). Report odds ratios with CIs to quantify effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of peer-reviewed journal article as baseline
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the text of the associated peer-reviewed journal article as the baseline against which press releases and news are compared for exaggeration, advice level, causal claims, and human inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge limitations: the journal article may itself contain exaggeration or be ambiguous; the method records deviations beyond the journal text rather than absolute accuracy. If feasible, supplement baseline comparisons with expert judgment of paper results.
